author: Amy V. Margaris, Mark A. Rusk, Patrick G. Saltonstall and Molly Odell
annotation: Combines archaeological evidence and historical records to interpret a small seasonal company work camp. Its analysis distinguishes imposed labor from workers' continuing skills and choices. Conclusions are a site-specific interpretation, not proof of identical conditions in every Alutiiq community.
publicationDate: 2015; Arctic Anthropology 52(1):102–126
contentReviewScope: Selected actual article text: introduction and colonial-labor passages, printed pages 102–105; Discussion and Conclusions passages, pages 121–123. Oberlin metadata verified; full-text host identifies upload by Amy Margaris on August 10, 2015.

author: Edward H. Spicer
type: Academic / historical ethnography with attributed recollections
citation: Spicer, Edward H. 1940. Pascua: A Yaqui Village in Arizona. Chicago: University of Chicago Press. Chapter I, selected History paragraphs. Open Arizona reprint, University of Arizona Press, May 2019, ISBN 9780816540327.
annotation: Spicer places migration memories within his study of Pascua, Arizona, including an El Paso crossing recollection. This outside anthropologist’s mediated local account does not corroborate the Texas Band’s specific Presidio/Fort Davis narrative.
countReason: One partial substantive book review: multiple complete History paragraphs actually read from the indexed publisher chapter body, beyond the search-summary snippets. The record and reprint are not separate works.
contentReviewScope: Chapter I: History opening paragraph (including Francisco Valencia’s reported El Paso crossing), following historical-context/migration paragraphs, and selected Yaquis in Arizona/local-founding paragraphs; Population opening establishes the May 1937 study context, and Summary opening was read. The indexed body omits intervening text, so this is noncontinuous selected content, not a complete chapter or book review. No printed pagination was available in the inspected HTML; none is invented.
perspective: An outside anthropologist’s 1940 interpretation, based on residents’ recollections and other literature. The El Paso story is mediated and undated in the selected passage; underlying interviews and crossing records were not inspected.
accessStatus: Publisher-designated open-access English reprint; selected substantial indexed chapter body inspected
accessNotes: Normal chapter retrieval returned a JavaScript reader shell (HTTP 200), while search exposed substantial primary-publisher chapter text. Only the selected body is claimed as inspected; this was not a paywall or challenge bypass. Full-book text, maps, images, raw interviews and a paginated PDF were not inspected. Historical population, racial classifications, blanket migration/language claims and culturally governed descriptions were excluded from synthesis.
rightsNotes: Link and brief attributed paraphrase only. Open access does not by itself establish permission to reproduce the book or illustrations; no reuse license is claimed.

annotation: This 2010 Spanish-language book chapter surveys Kickapoo histories from the Great Lakes to Coahuila and Texas and discusses the formation of the Texas community, cross-border relations, land, federal recognition, and the Lucky Eagle casino context. title: Ethnic Consciousness in Cultural Survival: The Morongo Band of Mission Indians and the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas
publisher: Elisabeth A. Mager; translation by Heather Dashner Monk; American Indian Culture and Research Journal / eScholarship, University of California
annotation: This peer-reviewed comparative study includes a dedicated section on the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas and El Nacimiento. Mager identifies documentary research, participant observation, and interviews as methods and cites interviews conducted from 1995 to 2015, along with the Texas Tribe’s 1981–1984 Land Acquisition Committee report. Selected passages discuss land acquisition and economic history; the author’s theory of “ethnic consciousness,” causal claims, and generalizations remain her interpretation, not a community consensus. This is the same researcher represented by sources 6 and 11, so repeated claims are not independent corroboration. Cultural descriptions outside the selected historical scope were not used.
contentReviewScope: Read article metadata and research-method statement (printed pp.47–48), Kickapoo-focused land and Texas economic-history passages (printed pp.61–63), and the corresponding cited notes on printed p.71. The comparative sections about Morongo and detailed ceremonial/cultural descriptions were not used. Claims are attributed to the author and the dates/interview sources stated in her notes.

title: No-ko-aht’s Talk: A Kickapoo Chief’s Account of a Tribal Journey from Kansas to Mexico and Return in the Sixties
publisher: George A. Root, editor; Kansas Historical Society; account recorded by Franklin G. Adams
annotation: The article prints a May 31, 1867 account attributed to Kickapoo leader No-ko-aht and recorded in shorthand by federal agent Franklin G. Adams. No-ko-aht describes travel between Kansas and Mexico, the 1865 Dove Creek conflict, life in Coahuila, and his objections to treaty pressure and settler encroachment. This is a historically valuable but mediated account: the recorder was a federal agent, George A. Root edited and published it in 1932, and the surrounding editorial narrative uses period terminology and makes claims that should not be adopted as neutral fact. The printed account and editorial summary also differ in chronology and group counts; the discrepancy is retained rather than reconciled here.

title: Grand Portage Band Regains Historic Tribal Land
author: Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Chippewa
publisher: Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Chippewa
type: Tribal news release / contemporary land stewardship
publicationDate: March 16, 2026
contentReviewScope: Read the full 83-line public Band news release on October 23, 2026. It reports the February 16, 2026 acquisition of three parcels through a Band/Foundation partnership, describes the Band account of different land-loss mechanisms, and quotes the Band chair and partner representatives. Its linked map/images were not opened or used. The Band statements about federal policy and the parcels past ownership are attributed community interpretation; underlying treaty, land-title and allotment records were not independently inspected.
annotation: A Grand Portage Band news release reports that a February 2026 acquisition restored three parcels totaling about 87 acres to Band ownership through a partnership with the Lloyd K. Johnson Foundation and Minnesota Land Trust. The Band describes three distinct routes by which those parcels left Band ownership: 1854 treaty cession, state school-trust transfer, and allotment. This is a direct community source for the Bands current action and its historical interpretation; the underlying treaty, land-title chain, tax records, and allotment documents were not independently checked. The Bands broad discussion of allotment policy remains attributed to the release and is not generalized to every Ojibwe Band. A linked map/images package is not included.

title: Presidio Los Adaes: Spanish, French, and Caddoan Interaction on the Northern Frontier
publisher: Historical Archaeology 38(3), pp. 65–77 · Society for Historical Archaeology; authorized Texas Beyond History copy
author: H. F. Gregory, George Avery, Aubra L. Lee, and Jay C. Blaine
annotation: Actual scanned article visually inspected at printed pp. 65, 67–71, and 74–75, including the excavation overview and conclusions. Compares documentary expectations with Indigenous pottery, French and Spanish goods, architecture, and food remains at the presidio. Material patterns concern a mixed colonial settlement; they do not identify every maker as Adai or prove equal power and universal harmony. Site-specific counts and social interpretations need their original contexts. This authored journal study is distinct from the later public exhibit.

title: El sistema fonológico del Kickapoo de Coahuila analizado desde las metodologías distribucional y funcional
publisher: José Luis Moctezuma Zamarrón and Fernando Nava López; Instituto Nacional de Lenguas Indígenas (INALI)
annotation: A substantial Spanish-language study combines a short ethnographic overview of the El Nacimiento community with two phonological analyses of the Coahuila variety and a chapter on a practical writing system. The author reports six months of fieldwork in 1980–1983 and later visits in 1988 and 2010; a later chapter describes consultation and community decision-making in developing a practical alphabet. These are dated, author-attributed observations, not a measure of present language use or a universal account of every Kickapoo community. Restricted cultural descriptions were excluded from the atlas synthesis.
contentReviewScope: Selected sections in the 146-page PDF: printed pages 13–23 (method, community geography/history and economic context), 30–45 (social organization, language-use description), and 109–120 (practical alphabet). Other chapters and restricted cultural descriptions were not used.

title: Leech Lake Band of Chippewa Indians v. Herbst, 334 F. Supp. 1001 (D. Minn. 1971)
author: U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota, Chief Judge Edward J. Devitt
publisher: Justia, reproducing a reported federal district-court opinion
sourceKind: Reported U.S. District Court memorandum and order
publicationDate: December 10, 1971
topics: Treaty fishing, hunting, and wild-rice rights
annotation: The complete reported opinion addresses whether Leech Lake Band members could fish, hunt, and gather wild rice on public lands and waters within the Leech Lake Reservation free from Minnesota game and fish laws. The court held that treaty rights had not been abrogated by the Nelson Act and declared those activities protected on the specified public lands and waters. The opinion did not accept the Band’s claim to exclusive regulatory authority over all fishing, hunting, and ricing. This is a dated judicial holding in a particular case, not a statement of current regulations or a substitute for later law.
contentReviewScope: Read the full opinion and notes (reported text at pages 1001–1010; Justia lines 38–143). The opinion recounts the litigants’ positions, testimony, treaty/legal analysis, and the court’s narrow declaratory judgment. The 1855/1864/1867 treaty originals, trial exhibits, and later proceedings were not independently inspected in this entry.

title: State v. Forge, 262 N.W.2d 341 (Minn. 1977)
author: Supreme Court of Minnesota
publisher: Justia, reproducing a reported Minnesota Supreme Court opinion
publicationDate: October 14, 1977
annotation: The full opinion recounts the Leech Lake Band’s 1969 federal lawsuit, the 1971 Herbst decision, the 1973 settlement and consent judgment, and challenges to Minnesota’s reservation fishing stamp. The Minnesota Supreme Court held that Minnesota Chippewa Tribe members retained treaty rights and upheld the 1973 statutory compromise and the convictions of nonmembers who fished without the stamp. This later ruling supplies important historical context for the 1971 opinion; it does not establish every present-day regulation or decide all treaty-right questions.
contentReviewScope: Read the full reported opinion and notes (262 N.W.2d 341–349; Justia lines 38–163), including its description of the 1971 federal case, the 1973 settlement and consent judgment, statutory terms, holding, and express limits on what issues the appeal decided. The settlement document, current statute and later court cases were not separately reviewed.

title: Fond du Lac Band of Lake Superior Chippewa v. Cummins et al., Document 48 (D. Minn. Feb. 24, 2023)
author: United States District Court for the District of Minnesota; Chief Judge Patrick J. Schiltz
publisher: Justia, reproducing the federal district-court order
sourceKind: District-court order denying a motion to dismiss
publicationDate: February 24, 2023
annotation: In a challenge to a Forest Service land exchange for the proposed NorthMet mine, the District Court denied PolyMet’s motion to dismiss. At this pleading-stage ruling, it accepted the complaint’s allegation that the exchange could remove access to 6,650 acres used for the Band’s treaty rights and held that the Band had standing to assert its own 1854 Treaty usufructuary interests; those rights were not exclusively individual member rights. This is not a decision on the merits of the land exchange or the ultimate project outcome. The alleged access loss is described as a complaint allegation, not a factual finding.
contentReviewScope: Read the full 18-page opinion as reproduced on Justia, including the docket/date and disposition (lines 38–50), the complaint’s background and stated alleged injury (lines 51–63), the treaty and tribal-right analysis (lines 64–98), and the order denying dismissal (lines 103–110). The complaint and docket exhibits, Forest Service Record of Decision, environmental review, and later case history were not independently inspected.

title: 2025 Strategic Tribal Transportation Safety Plan
publisher: Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas; prepared with Red Plains Professional
annotation: A public planning document prepared for the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas with consultant Red Plains Professional. It records a 2024 safety-planning grant, coordination among Tribal departments and outside safety partners, and proposed outreach and transportation-safety strategies. The text calls for some media to use or honor Tribal/local language, symbols, or culture. It is evidence of a dated planning process and stated strategies, not proof that proposed actions were completed or a general account of Kickapoo culture. The 127-page PDF includes digital appendices and an earlier plan; this guide does not reproduce crash data, locations, or appendices.
contentReviewScope: Read the 2025 plan’s title, contents, vision/introduction, plan-development and safety-partner sections (printed pp. 1–4), and selected education, outreach, data-management, and implementation sections (printed pp. 34–41). The appendices, underlying crash records, exact location data, web GIS application, and 2015 plan were not inspected.
accessNotes: Public PDF hosted on the Tribe’s official website. No reuse license was identified; the atlas links to the document and does not reproduce its maps or data.

title: Constitution of the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas, with scanned amendment and federal election/approval records
publisher: Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas; U.S. Department of the Interior, Bureau of Indian Affairs
annotation: The Tribe-hosted 20-page scan includes the constitution and BIA election/approval papers from 1989, 2017, and 2018. The preamble describes organization as a Tribe separate and apart from the Kickapoo Tribe of Oklahoma; the 1989 approval certificate states that its approval does not authorize action contrary to federal law. Later papers document amendments to constitutional provisions. The scan’s cover wording and included amendment-number labels are not fully consistent, and it is not independently verified here as the currently operative consolidated constitution. It is a primary historical/governance record, not legal advice or a source for private enrollment details.
publicationDate: 1989 constitution; amendment/election papers 2017 and 2018
contentReviewScope: Scanned PDF pages 1–3 and 14–20 visually inspected: preamble, jurisdiction/governance passages, 1989 approval certificate, amendment text, and BIA election/approval records. Individual names/rolls and membership criteria were not transcribed.
accessNotes: Publicly downloadable scan on the Tribe’s official website; image-based PDF rather than searchable text.

These are the community website’s retrospective descriptions, not independently inspected building or program records, precise dates for every activity, present services or measured outcomes. This specifically named Kitigan Zibi account remains distinct from the Pikwàkanagàn and Ardoch examples.
publicationDate: Undated; the ©2021 site footer does not date the historical prose.
dateBasis: The source displays dated historical leadership-section headings and institutional-event years, but no personal narrative byline, prose publication date or revision date was established. The site footer is not adopted as a publication date.
contentReviewScope: Actual public HTML selected the community-center opening and public club-use clauses in the section headed John B. Chabot; the autumn-1957 rebuilding clause under William Commanda; and arts/crafts training, marketing, language-teacher preparation and grammar-project clauses under the 1970–1976 heading. The heading supplies a period for the latter account, not exact dates for each initiative. Original records, source photographs and the grammar were not inspected.
countReason: One explanatory institutional history selected for several connected community-building, arts and language-education passages. Not one work per leader, period, paragraph or initiative.
perspective: Kitigan Zibi’s public institutional retrospective; section headings name historical leaders, not established prose authors. No current office, recognition, membership, territory or equivalence with other Algonquin communities is determined.
accessStatus: Public exact-URL readable English HTML; normal reader received the historical body

title: Materials Related to the Co-Management of the Chippewa National Forest: The Right to Self-Governance — Historical and Current Overview of the Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe
author: Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe, Division of Resource Management
publicationDate: Undated compilation; contains a 2019 Memorandum of Understanding and a 2020 briefing presentation
annotation: A first-party Leech Lake Band educational and resource-management account, created to explain historical events, treaties, the Band’s government, and its agency relationships to Band staff and citizens. The historical overview narrates the 1837, 1854, 1855, 1864, and 1867 treaty sequence, later allotment and logging, the 1898 Sugar Point conflict, and the Band’s resource-governance work. Treaty-right and legal conclusions are presented as the Band’s institutional interpretation; the underlying treaty instruments, court opinions, and cited historical records were not independently checked in this source review. The booklet also includes later co-management materials that should be read as dated documents, not assumed to describe every current policy.
contentReviewScope: Read the complete first 20-page “Right to Self-Governance: Historical and Current Overview” (PDF pages 4–23), including its preface, treaty chronology, Nelson Act/allotment and timber discussion, Sugar Point account, present governance and federal/state-agency relationships. The complete PDF has 133 pages; later slide decks, the 2019 MOU, appendices, management letters, implementation guide, and species list were not inspected as separate works. No map or sensitive site information was reused.

author: Annie Rosenthal
publicationDate: April 19, 2024

annotation: Annie Rosenthal reports on the completion of a community-led protection and interpretation project at a Presidio cemetery. Interviewed descendants, an anthropologist, the Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas vice-chairman, local conservation partners, and the project architect describe their different roles. The story reports that a descendant drafted historical-marker text in collaboration with the Texas Historical Commission and that the completed site includes public historical and cultural interpretation. Use it as a dated local case study of contemporary community stewardship, not as a complete account of the Tribe or of Lipan communities generally. The profile summarizes the public-history work and omits sensitive burial details.

title: Mescalero Apache Tribe commemorates reservation boundaries created 150 years ago
author: Mescalero Apache Tribe; institutional byline
publicationDate: June 6, 2023
annotation: The Tribe’s own 2023 commemoration describes its communitywide anniversary event for the present reservation boundaries and quotes then-President Edward Martinez explaining the Tribe’s interpretation of the 1873 designation. The article describes the contemporary Tribe as comprising Mescalero, Lipan, and Chiricahua bands and gives a Lipan arrival date of 1905, while the Tribe’s undated Our Culture page says “about 1903”; that discrepancy is left open. Statements about time immemorial and ancestry are attributed to the Tribe or its president, not independently established by this article.
contentReviewScope: Read the full visible article body, especially the Tribe’s account of the 1873 anniversary, the quoted statement from President Edward Martinez, its description of three constituent bands, and the 1905 Lipan / 1913 Chiricahua chronology (lines 13–34). The linked resolution and parade video were not opened; ceremonial activity is not described beyond the article’s public event summary.

The publication and its introduction reflect two different periods of outsider authorship.

The Atlas does not reproduce curriculum materials, participant data, images, or private content.

title: Idaho v. United States, 533 U.S. 262
publisher: Supreme Court of the United States
annotation: Read the opinion in volume 533, pp. 262–280 (bound PDF pp. 265–280 in an 868-page volume). The Court held that the United States holds in trust for the Tribe the specified submerged lands within the reservation, including portions of the lake and river. The holding is limited to title in the disputed submerged lands; it is not a ruling that the Tribe owns the whole lake or every basin interest.

title: TxDOT Tribal Histories: Ysleta del Sur Pueblo Research Report
author: TxDOT Tribal Histories Project research team, developed in consultation with Ysleta del Sur Pueblo’s Department of Cultural Preservation
annotation: A 2021 TxDOT research report prepared for transportation planning and public education. Its introduction says the source set was recommended and approved by Ysleta del Sur Pueblo’s Director of Cultural Preservation, who also commented on the draft. The report combines historical scholarship, archival material, community publications, oral history and GIS work. These are a named community member’s reported perspectives, not independently verified archaeological conclusions or a statement for every Atakapa/Ishak community. title: Memorial of the Tonkawa Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma relating to claims against the United States — S. Doc. 60-206
publisher: Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma; printed by the U.S. Senate in the Congressional Serial Set
author: Memorial adopted by the Tonkawa Tribe at Oakland Agency on January 2, 1907; member affidavits and historical extracts appended
type: Primary community petition and member testimony in a congressional record
publicationDate: Memorial adopted January 2, 1907; presented to Senate January 28, 1908
annotation: This six-page Senate document reproduces a memorial adopted by the Tonkawa Tribe in council and affidavits from members contesting the 1891 cession’s terms and the way it was negotiated. Their claims are direct evidence of the Tribe’s later position and named members’ recollections, not a judicial finding or independent valuation. The memorial’s account should be read alongside the 1892 federal document, which records commissioners’ contrasting assessment. It also reprints older federal agent reports with their own colonial and comparative framing; those passages are attributed rather than adopted.
contentReviewScope: Read all six PDF pages, including the council memorial, affidavits by Frank E. Mason, John Rush Buffalo, and John Allen, and appended excerpts from federal agents’ reports. Claims about the negotiation are attributed to the memorialists and affiants; the appended agent language is not treated as Tonkawa testimony. No individualized allotment or burial site details were published.

profileContexts.publisher: U.S. Geological Survey, prepared in cooperation with the Kootenai Tribe of Idaho
profileContexts.annotation: A technical evaluation of a Kootenai Tribe-led, interagency restoration program in the Kootenai River’s Braided and Straight Reaches. Selected findings report improved pool and depth metrics after construction, but the tested conditions did not meet the stated channel-depth target, and sediment trends did not show that the treatments themselves reduced suspended-sediment transport. The study is geographically and methodologically bounded; it does not evaluate the Tribe’s overall stewardship or establish species recovery.

The official publication record returned 403 to one automated page fetch, but the linked USGS PDF downloaded successfully; this is not described as a reader paywall.

title: Tonkawa Indians at Fort Griffin, Texas — H. Ex. Doc. 44-102
author: U.S. House of Representatives; correspondence by War Department, Interior Department, and Army officers
publisher: U.S. Government Publishing Office, Congressional Serial Set; digitized by the Law Library of Congress
type: Primary government correspondence / Congressional Serial Set document
publicationDate: February 1, 1876; compiles correspondence from 1872–1876
contentReviewScope: Read the full searchable text of the eight-page public PDF, including its letters and reports dated 1872–1876. The OCR text was inspected; the page images, handwriting, signatures, and original correspondence files were not independently inspected. The authors write from federal and military administrative positions, not as Tonkawa or Lipan narrators. No reader access restriction was encountered.
annotation: The congressional document records federal officials’ accounts of a small Lipan group moving from Fort Sill to Fort Griffin in 1874, subsequent ration decisions affecting Tonkawa and Lipan people there, and proposed removal options. The 1875 Interior Department letter reports kinship through intermarriage and discusses a possible consolidation; it is an official’s account and recommendation, not a Lipan-authored history or evidence that the proposal was implemented. It must not be generalized to all Lipan people or treated as proof of incorporation into Mescalero Apache.

title: Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma v. Richards, No. 94-50369 (corrected opinion following rehearing)
author: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit; opinion by Judge Robert M. Parker
publisher: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
type: Federal appellate opinion / primary legal record
annotation: The corrected February 9, 1996 appellate opinion recounts the Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma’s suit over the 1866 Texas act, which provided for a one-league home site selected by the Governor. The Fifth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Texas and held that the act did not create a perfected, self-executing grant under the record and statutory language before the panel. The decision addresses that statute and case; it is not a general historical-homeland survey, a statement about present Tonkawa identity, or current legal advice. The court states that the opinion replaced its October 1995 version after rehearing to correct a factual error; only the corrected text is used here.
contentReviewScope: Read the official 20-page opinion’s opening and procedural history, its reproduction of the 1864 resolution and 1866 act, the background to the Tribe’s later claim, the statutory and Nonintercourse Act analysis, the court’s conclusion, and the rehearing correction (PDF pp. 1–5, 8–10, 12–17, 20). The underlying 1866 legislative record, district-court docket, original 1992–1994 correspondence, and later treatment of the ruling were not independently checked. Historical facts recounted by the opinion remain attributed to the court and cited sources.
publicationDate: Corrected opinion filed February 9, 1996; substituted after rehearing for the October 23, 1995 opinion
